title: Subject-verb agreement
blurb: Find the true subject in any sentence and match the verb to it, even past phrases, pronouns like each, either/or pairs and inverted order.
question: A clinic newsletter reads, “The list of new patient forms, along with the updated consent policies, are on the front desk.” Is the verb correct, and how do you prove it in under a minute on test day?

teach.h: The verb matches its subject, nothing else
teach.body: Formally, a verb must agree with its subject in number: a singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. Plain English: find the one word the sentence is really about, decide whether it is one or more than one, and make the verb match. In the present tense the s usually flips: a singular subject gets the verb with -s (the nurse checks), and a plural subject drops it (the nurses check).

teach.h: Phrases between subject and verb do not count
teach.body: Prepositional phrases (of the patients, in the cabinet) and add-on phrases (along with, as well as, together with, in addition to) never change the subject. “One of the patients has a fever”: the subject is one, so has. “The surgeon, along with two residents, is scrubbing in”: only and makes a compound subject; along with does not. Cross the phrase out and the answer is obvious.

teach.h: Subjects that look plural but are singular

rows.label: Five hundred dollars is the fee.
The news from the lab is good.
“Lean on Me” is her favorite song.
The number of applicants is rising.
A number of applicants are waiting.

teach.note: In US English, collective nouns (team, staff, committee, family, class, jury) take a singular verb when they act as one unit.

teach.body: When the verb comes before the subject, the subject is hiding after it. In “There are three unsigned forms,” the subject is forms, not there. In “On the counter sit two bags of saline,” the subject is bags. Turn the sentence around (“Two bags of saline sit on the counter”) and match the verb. Here and there are never the subject.

Nursing applicant Jasmine Ortiz volunteers on a clinic newsletter. She reads: “The list of new patient forms, along with the updated consent policies, are on the front desk.” Step 1: cross out “of new patient forms” and “along with the updated consent policies.” Step 2: the subject is list. Step 3: list is singular. Step 4: “The list ... is on the front desk.” She changes are to is.

teach.text: The classic HESI A2 trap puts a plural noun right before the verb (“The list of supplies were”) so the verb sounds right. Agree with the true subject (list), not with the nearest noun. The same trap appears with each and everyone, which look like groups but are always singular.

items: Cross out phrases between subject and verb; along with and as well as do not make a subject plural.
And makes a plural subject; with or, nor, either/or and neither/nor, match the nearer subject.
Each, every, either, neither, one and every -one/-body/-thing word is singular; both, few, many, several are plural.
Some, any, none, all, most, more: match the noun after of.
Collective nouns acting as a unit, amounts, titles and news take singular verbs; “the number” is singular, “a number” is plural.
In inverted order (There are, Here is), find the subject after the verb.

summary: You can now strip away phrases to find the true subject and match the verb to it. You can also handle compound subjects, indefinite pronouns, collective nouns, amounts and inverted sentences the way the HESI A2 expects.

A.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “The results of Mr. Okafor's blood test ___ ready for review.”
A.why: The subject is results (plural); “of Mr. Okafor's blood test” is a phrase in between. Plural subject, plural verb: “The results ... are ready.”

whyNot.0: Is agrees with test, the noun inside the prepositional phrase, not with the subject results.
whyNot.2: Has been is singular; the plural subject results needs have been.
whyNot.3: Was is singular; the plural subject results needs were (or are).

A.q: Which sentence uses correct subject-verb agreement?
options: Each of the new nurses have a locker key.
Every one of the students were given a badge.
Someone in the two classes have a spare key.
Everyone on both shifts has a locker key.
A.why: Everyone is an indefinite pronoun that is always singular, so it takes has. The phrase “on both shifts” does not change that.

whyNot.0: Each is always singular, so it needs has, not have. “Of the new nurses” is a phrase in between.
whyNot.1: Every one is singular, so the verb should be was given.
whyNot.2: Someone is always singular, so the verb should be has; “in the two classes” is a phrase in between.

A.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “Neither the nursing students nor their instructor ___ allowed in the lab after 6 p.m.”
A.why: With neither ... nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Instructor is nearer and singular, so is.

whyNot.1: Are agrees with students, the farther subject. Neither/nor follows the nearer subject.
whyNot.2: Were is plural; the nearer subject, instructor, is singular.
whyNot.3: Have been is plural; the nearer subject, instructor, needs has been or is.

B.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “The admissions committee ___ its decision every Friday.”
B.why: In US English a collective noun acting as one unit takes a singular verb. The singular pronoun its confirms the committee is acting as one body: announces.

whyNot.0: Announce is the plural form; committee acting as a unit is singular.
whyNot.1: Are announcing is plural; it would also clash with the singular its.
whyNot.3: Have announced is plural; the singular form would be has announced.

B.q: Which sentence from a clinic memo uses correct agreement?
options: Here is the lab results you asked for.
There are two messages from the pharmacy.
On the counter sits three bags of saline.
There's several reasons to arrive early.
B.why: In inverted order the subject follows the verb. The subject is messages (plural), so there are is correct.

whyNot.0: The subject is results (plural), so it should be “Here are the lab results.”
whyNot.2: The subject is bags (plural), so it should be “On the counter sit three bags.”
whyNot.3: There's means there is, but the subject reasons is plural: “There are several reasons.”

B.q: Which sentence about the lab supplies is grammatically correct?
options: All of the saline have been used.
Some of the vials is past the expiration date.
None of the paperwork were completed on time.
Most of the samples are labeled correctly.
B.why: Most is a SANAM pronoun, so it matches the noun after of. Samples is plural, so are is correct.

whyNot.0: Saline is uncountable, so all of the saline is singular: has been used.
whyNot.1: Vials is plural, so some of the vials takes are.
whyNot.2: Paperwork is uncountable, so none of the paperwork takes was.

C.q: Which sentence follows the rules of subject-verb agreement?
options: The box of masks is on the top shelf.
Fifty dollars are the fee for the retake.
The news from the lab are encouraging.
Each of the counties are reporting cases.
C.why: Cross out “of masks”: the subject is box, which is singular, so is.

whyNot.1: An amount of money treated as one sum is singular: “Fifty dollars is the fee.”
whyNot.2: News is singular despite the -s: “The news ... is encouraging.”
whyNot.3: Each is singular, so it needs is reporting; “of the counties” is a phrase in between.

C.q: Dana's draft reads: “The number of applicants to the program have doubled, and a number of them is from out of state.” Which pair of verbs makes the sentence correct?
C.why: “The number of” is singular (one number), so has doubled. “A number of” means several, so it is plural: a number of them are.

whyNot.0: “The number” is a single figure, so it needs has doubled, not have doubled.
whyNot.2: “A number of them” means many people, so it needs the plural are.
whyNot.3: Both verbs are wrong: the number takes has; a number of them takes are.

C.q: Which sentence contains a subject-verb agreement error?
options: Neither the aides nor the nurse is on break.
Either the residents or the doctor signs the order.
The cost of the new monitors were too high.
Each of the rooms has its own sink.
C.why: The subject is cost (singular); “of the new monitors” is a phrase in between. It should read “The cost ... was too high.”

whyNot.0: Correct: with neither/nor the verb matches the nearer subject, nurse, so is.
whyNot.1: Correct: with either/or the verb matches the nearer subject, doctor, so signs.
whyNot.3: Correct: each is singular, so has, and its matches each.

reteach.title: The verb only dances with its partner
reteach.question: Picture a crowded dance floor. The verb has exactly one partner, the subject, no matter who is standing between them. How do you spot the partner?

blocks.body: A sentence like “The bag of oranges on the shelves near the windows is heavy” has a crowd of nouns: oranges, shelves, windows. They are bystanders. The verb's partner is bag, the word the sentence is about. If the partner is one person, the verb dances solo (is, has, checks). If the partner is a group, the verb joins the group (are, have, check). Two partners joined by and make a group; with or/nor, the verb dances with whoever is standing closest.

blocks.text: The bystander standing right next to the verb is the one that fools you. Always read the subject and verb together with the crowd removed: “The bag ... is.”

explain.body: Cross out every prepositional phrase (of, in, on, for) and add-on phrase (along with, as well as, together with). What is left before the verb is the subject. Match the verb to that word alone.

test.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “The supply of flu vaccines for the three clinics ___ running low.”
test.why: Cross out “of flu vaccines for the three clinics”: the subject is supply, which is singular, so is.

whyNot.0: Are agrees with vaccines or clinics, which are inside phrases.
whyNot.1: Have been is plural; supply needs has been.
whyNot.2: Were is plural; supply needs was.

explain.body: Two subjects joined by and are plural. Two subjects joined by or, nor, either ... or, or neither ... nor take the verb that matches the nearer one. Put the plural subject second and the sentence also sounds natural.

test.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “Either the pharmacist or the nurses ___ the patient's questions about side effects.”
test.why: With either ... or, the verb matches the nearer subject. Nurses is plural, so answer.

whyNot.0: Answers agrees with pharmacist, the farther subject.
whyNot.1: Has answered is singular; nurses needs have answered.
whyNot.3: Is answering is singular; nurses needs are answering.

explain.body: Each, every, either, neither, one and every word ending in -one, -body or -thing are singular. Both, few, many, several and others are plural. Some, any, none, all, most and more (SANAM) follow the noun after of.

test.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “Everybody in the two study groups ___ a practice test on Thursday.”
test.why: Everybody is always singular, so it takes the singular verb takes. “In the two study groups” is a phrase in between.

whyNot.1: Take is the plural form; everybody is singular.
whyNot.2: Are taking is plural; everybody needs is taking.
whyNot.3: Have taken is plural; everybody needs has taken.

explain.body: Collective nouns acting as a unit, amounts, titles and the -s noun news take singular verbs (a few -s nouns, such as measles and economics, can take either). In sentences that start with There, Here or a phrase, find the subject after the verb.

test.q: Which sentence matches its special subject to the correct verb?
options: The jury have reached its verdict.
The team has its meeting at noon.
There is two exits on this floor.
Twenty minutes are the time limit.
test.why: Team is a collective noun acting as one unit, so the singular has matches it (and its).

whyNot.0: Jury acting as one unit (its verdict) needs the singular has.
whyNot.2: The subject is exits (plural), so There are.
whyNot.3: A span of time treated as one amount is singular: Twenty minutes is the time limit.
